items.title: fix(launch): drop whole audit records at the byte budget
items.body:
Fixes #186

## Summary

- `audit_write` now collects the fragments of one audit record in a 256-byte staging buffer and writes the record with a single `write` once its newline arrives. The budget is checked against the whole record: a record that does not fit is dropped entirely, and `ginux: audit truncated budget=65536` is always a line of its own.
- The longest record is about 150 bytes. A record that would overflow the staging buffer stops auditing with the same notice instead of writing part of it.
- Byte accounting is unchanged (only written bytes count), so the output stays below the existing 68000-byte check.

Details and reproduction: #186.

## Changes

- `crates/ginux-init/src/launch.rs`: `AUDIT_RECORD` staging buffer in `audit_write`, notice moved to `audit_cap`.
- `scripts/test-launch.py`: the `budget` case now also requires the notice as a line of its own and every `ginux: audit sequence=` line to be a complete entry or exit record.

## Testing

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check`, `make check` (incl. clippy), `make test-unit` | pass |
| `make test-launch` with this change | pass (stderr ends with `... sequence=438 phase=exit result=4242`, then `ginux: audit truncated budget=65536` on its own line) |
| `make test-launch` (with the new check) and `main`'s binary | fails: `ginux: audit sequence=439 phase=entry syscall=39ginux: audit truncated budget=65536` |
| `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

items.title: Enable overflow checks in release builds
items.body:
Addresses issue #43 without closing it.

This enables overflow checks for the workspace release profile and adds a release-mode regression that requires a runtime usize overflow to panic. The standard check target now runs that regression.

Checked-release boot testing exposed two eager rejected-branch underflows, which now use lazy conditional evaluation. The larger checked binaries also required bounded capacity updates: the root image publication limit is 164 pages, and the network image uses a canonical 161-page capacity shared by its loader and validator.

Verification:
- make check
- make test
- make test-qemu-smoke
- post-change EFI 70,135,296 bytes, +72,192 bytes or about 0.103%
- final cached smoke 9.54 seconds versus 9.22-second coarse baseline

Please keep issue #43 open until maintainer review. This PR does not merge or close anything.

items.title: File I/O ABI: pwrite/pwritev ignore O_APPEND and pwritev2 refuses RWF_(NO)APPEND; lseek SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE unsupported; fallocate refuses FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE and PUNCH_HOLE; ftruncate error order
items.body:
Hi, thank you for Ginux! While testing real container images I ran into the problem below. Everything is measured against Linux 7.3 on the same host.

### Measured

All values from `probe-27.py` (raw syscalls via ctypes unless noted). Linux column: host Linux 7.3, glibc Python, `/tmp` on tmpfs.

| Probe | Linux 7.3 | Ginux before | Ginux after |
|---|---|---|---|
| raw `pwrite64(fd,"XY",0)`, O_WRONLY\|O_APPEND, file `0123` | `0123XY` | **`XY23`** | `0123XY` |
| raw `pwritev(fd,["XY"],0)` on O_APPEND | `0123XY` | **`0XY3`** (offset 1) | `0123XY` |
| `pwritev2(…, 1, RWF_NOAPPEND)` on O_APPEND | 2, `0XY3` | ENOTSUP | 2, `0XY3` |
| `pwritev2(…, 0, RWF_APPEND)` without O_APPEND | 2, `0123XY` | ENOTSUP | 2, `0123XY` |
| `pwritev2(…, RWF_APPEND\|RWF_NOAPPEND)` | EINVAL | ENOTSUP | EINVAL |
| raw `pwrite64(fd, …, -1)` | EINVAL | ENOSPC | EINVAL |
| Python `os.pwrite(fd,b"XY",0)` on O_APPEND (libc `pwrite`) | `0123XY` (glibc) | **ENOTSUP** (musl) | `XY23` (musl, see note) |
| `lseek` 100-byte file: SEEK_DATA 0 / SEEK_HOLE 0 / SEEK_DATA 100 / SEEK_HOLE 200 | 0 / 100 / ENXIO / ENXIO | EINVAL ×4 | 0 / 100 / ENXIO / ENXIO |
| SEEK_DATA 50, SEEK_HOLE 50, SEEK_DATA 99, SEEK_HOLE 100 | 50, 100, 99, ENXIO | EINVAL ×4 | 50, 100, 99, ENXIO |
| SEEK_DATA −1, SEEK_HOLE −5, whence 5 | ENXIO, ENXIO, EINVAL | EINVAL ×3 | ENXIO, ENXIO, EINVAL |
| file position after SEEK_HOLE from 10 / after an ENXIO | 100 / 10 (unchanged) | 10 / 10 | 100 / 10 |
| empty file: SEEK_DATA 0, SEEK_HOLE 0 | ENXIO, ENXIO | EINVAL, EINVAL | ENXIO, ENXIO |
| image file (`/etc/shells`): SEEK_DATA 0, SEEK_HOLE 0 = size, SEEK_DATA size | 0, size, ENXIO | EINVAL ×3 | 0, size, ENXIO |
| `fallocate` mode 0 grow 0..32 | 0, size 32 | 0, size 32 | 0, size 32 |
| `fallocate(KEEP_SIZE, 0, 64)` | 0, size 32 | **ENOTSUP** | 0, size 32 |
| `fallocate(KEEP_SIZE\|PUNCH_HOLE, 2, 2)` on `abcdefgh` | 0, `ab\0\0efgh` | **ENOTSUP**, unchanged | 0, `ab\0\0efgh` |
| `fallocate(PUNCH_HOLE)` without KEEP_SIZE / `ZERO_RANGE` | ENOTSUP / ENOTSUP | ENOTSUP / ENOTSUP | ENOTSUP / ENOTSUP |
| KEEP_SIZE past EOF (100+50) on 8-byte file, then append `Z` | 0, size 8 → 9 | ENOTSUP, 8 → 9 | 0, size 8 → 9 |
| punch 6..26 across EOF / 100..110 past EOF / 0..1 MiB | 0, `abcdef\0\0`, size 8 / 0 / 0, all zero, size 8 | ENOTSUP ×3, data unchanged | same as Linux |
| image file (`/etc/issue`) O_RDWR: KEEP_SIZE, punch 0..2 | 0, 0, size same, 2 bytes zero, rest same | ENOTSUP, ENOTSUP | 0, 0, size same, 2 bytes zero, rest same |
| unknown bit / NO_HIDE_STALE / COLLAPSE / INSERT / UNSHARE / KEEP\|ZERO / COLLAPSE\|KEEP / PUNCH\|ZERO | ENOTSUP ×8 | ENOTSUP ×8 | ENOTSUP ×8 |
| neg offset / neg len / offset+len overflow | EINVAL / EINVAL / EFBIG | EINVAL / EINVAL / EFBIG | EINVAL / EINVAL / EFBIG |
| bad fd / bad fd with len 0 | EBADF / EBADF | EBADF / EBADF | EBADF / EBADF |
| O_RDONLY fd: len 0 / unknown bit / PUNCH without KEEP | EINVAL / ENOTSUP / ENOTSUP | **EBADF ×3** | EINVAL / ENOTSUP / ENOTSUP |
| O_RDONLY fd: ZERO_RANGE / KEEP_SIZE / PUNCH\|KEEP / mode 0 | EBADF ×4 | EBADF ×4 | EBADF ×4 |
| pipe write end / pipe read end / directory | ESPIPE / EBADF / EBADF | **EROFS** / EBADF / EBADF | ESPIPE / EBADF / EBADF |
| `ftruncate` on O_RDONLY fd (`os.ftruncate`) | EINVAL | **EBADF** | EINVAL |
| `ftruncate` O_RDONLY len −1 / bad fd / bad fd len −1 | EINVAL / EBADF / EINVAL | EBADF / EBADF / EBADF | EINVAL / EBADF / EINVAL |
| `ftruncate` pipe write end / pipe read end / directory / O_PATH | EINVAL / EINVAL / EINVAL / EBADF | EROFS / EBADF / EBADF / EBADF | EINVAL / EINVAL / EINVAL / EBADF |
| `ftruncate` O_WRONLY len −1 / len 3 | EINVAL / 0, size 3 | EINVAL / 0, size 3 | EINVAL / 0, size 3 |
| FIFO `open(O_WRONLY\|O_NONBLOCK)` with no reader | **ENXIO** | 0 | 0 (not fixed) |
| FIFO O_RDWR\|O_NONBLOCK / O_RDONLY\|O_NONBLOCK without writer / O_WRONLY\|O_NONBLOCK with reader | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| FIFO O_WRONLY\|O_NONBLOCK after all fds closed | ENXIO | 0 | 0 (not fixed) |

Note on `os.pwrite`: musl's `pwrite()` issues `pwritev2(…, RWF_NOAPPEND)`; if that fails with EOPNOTSUPP and the descriptor has O_APPEND, musl returns EOPNOTSUPP itself instead of calling `pwrite64`. That is why Python's `os.pwrite` failed in Ginux while the raw `pwrite64` "worked" (at the wrong offset). With the patch musl gets RWF_NOAPPEND semantics, so it writes at the offset (`XY23`), which is the POSIX-2024 behaviour musl asks for. The host reference uses glibc, which calls `pwrite64` and appends (`0123XY`). We did not run musl on Linux; the musl-side behaviour is inferred from the before/after measurements and the raw `pwritev2(RWF_NOAPPEND)` row, which matches Linux.

Affected in practice: GNU `cp`/`tar`/`rsync` sparse-file handling and `lseek`-based copy loops (SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE), SQLite and other databases (`fallocate(KEEP_SIZE)` for preallocation), systemd-journald/`fallocate -p` (punch hole), any Alpine program using `pwrite()` on an O_APPEND file (log writers), and libraries that probe `ftruncate` error codes.

### Root cause

All in `kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs`:

- `linux_regular_file_write_at()` (pwrite64, and per-iovec for `linux_positioned_iov()` = preadv/pwritev/preadv2/pwritev2) always wrote at `offset`; `linux_positioned_iov()` returned EOPNOTSUPP for any `flags != 0`. No negative-offset check.
- `linux_regular_file_seek()` only knew whence 0, 1, 2.
- `linux_fallocate()` returned EOPNOTSUPP for every `mode != 0`, and checked the access mode first.
- `linux_ftruncate()` returned EBADF for every non-writable descriptor and checked the length after it. Pipes fell through to `linux_copy_up_descriptor()` → EROFS (same in `linux_fallocate()`).
- Named FIFOs (`linux_open_named_fifo()`) share one loopback socket per FIFO node (`linux_overlay::fifo_socket()`), reference-counted, with no reader/writer accounting.

### Linux rule

- `ksys_pwrite64()`: `pos < 0` → EINVAL before the fd lookup (`fs/read_write.c:796`). `generic_write_checks_count()`: with `IOCB_APPEND` the position becomes `i_size` (`fs/read_write.c:1758`); `IOCB_APPEND` comes from O_APPEND. `kiocb_set_rw_flags()`: RWF_APPEND and RWF_NOAPPEND together → EINVAL; RWF_NOAPPEND clears IOCB_APPEND (`include/linux/fs.h:3465, 3490`).
- `must_set_pos()` (used by `generic_file_llseek_size()`): SEEK_DATA → ENXIO if `(unsigned)offset >= eof`, else offset; SEEK_HOLE → ENXIO if `(unsigned)offset >= eof`, else eof (`fs/read_write.c:122-138`).
- `vfs_fallocate()`: `offset < 0 || len <= 0` → EINVAL; unknown bits or an invalid mode combination (PUNCH_HOLE without KEEP_SIZE; COLLAPSE/INSERT/ WRITE_ZEROES with KEEP_SIZE) → EOPNOTSUPP; then `!FMODE_WRITE` → EBADF; FIFO → ESPIPE; overflow → EFBIG (`fs/open.c:256-330`). `shmem_fallocate()` supports only KEEP_SIZE and PUNCH_HOLE (`mm/shmem.c:3634`); punch under F_SEAL_WRITE/FUTURE_WRITE → EPERM (`mm/shmem.c:3651`).
- `ksys_ftruncate()`: `length < 0` → EINVAL, then bad fd → EBADF (`fs/open.c:199-203`); `do_ftruncate()`: not a regular file or not FMODE_WRITE → EINVAL (`fs/open.c:170`). An O_PATH fd fails the fd lookup (EBADF).
- `fifo_open()`: O_WRONLY|O_NONBLOCK with no readers → ENXIO (`fs/pipe.c`).

### Fix

- `linux_regular_file_write_at()` now reads the descriptor's O_APPEND and calls the new `linux_regular_file_pwrite(…, append)`, which rejects a negative offset first and, with `append`, writes at the overlay file's size. `linux_positioned_iov()` accepts RWF_APPEND / RWF_NOAPPEND on writes as a per-call override (both → EINVAL); other flags stay EOPNOTSUPP.
- `linux_regular_file_seek()`: SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE as in `must_set_pos()` (files here have no holes: the whole file is data, the hole is at EOF); success updates the file position, ENXIO leaves it.
- `linux_fallocate()`: Linux's check order (EBADF closed/O_PATH → EINVAL range → EOPNOTSUPP mode → EBADF access → ESPIPE pipe → EFBIG), then the tmpfs-supported set. KEEP_SIZE keeps the size (nothing to reserve; the existing GROW-seal and RLIMIT_FSIZE checks still apply as in shmem). PUNCH_HOLE|KEEP_SIZE copies an image file up and writes zeros over the part of the range inside the file; the size never changes.
- `linux_ftruncate()`: length check first, EBADF only for a closed or O_PATH descriptor, EINVAL for a pipe or a non-writable descriptor.
- Constants `LINUX_ENXIO`, `LINUX_SEEK_DATA/HOLE`, `LINUX_FALLOC_FL_*`, `LINUX_RWF_APPEND/NOAPPEND` in `linux_abi.rs`.

Boot verification: `verify_linux_memfd_seals()` now also checks, on its 4-byte memfd, SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE/ENXIO, PUNCH_HOLE-without-KEEP_SIZE → EOPNOTSUPP, KEEP_SIZE, a KEEP_SIZE|PUNCH_HOLE that zeroes bytes 1..3 and an O_APPEND `pwrite` at offset 0 that appends (contents `d\0\0ad`), then restores the file before the existing seal checks. Its existing marker `ginux: Linux memfd sealing enforced across descriptors` (already asserted by `tests/qemu/boot.sh`) only prints if these pass.

### Not changed

- **FIFO `O_WRONLY|O_NONBLOCK` without a reader stays 0 instead of ENXIO.** A named FIFO is one shared, reference-counted loopback socket; there is no per-FIFO reader count. Getting ENXIO right needs reader accounting kept across open, dup, fork, exec (CLOEXEC) and close. That is not a small change and is left for a separate patch (the fork's 9f43c8c6 claims this).
- `open(O_APPEND)` sets the initial file position to the file size; Linux leaves it at 0 (`lseek(fd,0,SEEK_CUR)` after a pwrite on an O_APPEND fd: Linux 0, Ginux 4, before and after this patch). Separate issue, not touched.
- SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE report no holes inside sparse files (Linux tmpfs and ext4 do find them); this is the generic Linux behaviour and is correct for the overlay, which stores no holes.
- `fallocate(ZERO_RANGE)`, COLLAPSE, INSERT, UNSHARE stay EOPNOTSUPP like tmpfs.
- Reads with RWF_APPEND/RWF_NOAPPEND stay EOPNOTSUPP (Linux accepts and ignores them); fallocate/ftruncate on sockets are unchanged.

### Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| probe rows above (before → after) | match Linux except the FIFO rows (not fixed) and `os.pwrite` (glibc vs musl, see note) |
| `make check` | pass |
| `tests/qemu/boot.sh` under KVM (extended memfd checks) | "Boot test passed." |
| `QEMU_ACCEL=tcg tests/qemu/boot.sh` | "Boot test passed." |
| `git am` on clean `origin/main` + `make check` | applies, pass |

### For the reviewer

- Behaviour change: every positioned write on an O_APPEND descriptor now appends (pwrite64, pwritev, pwritev2 without flags, and the io_uring write path that calls `linux_regular_file_write_at()`), as on Linux.
- Hole punching writes zeros; it frees no memory.
- Textual overlap with PR #91: both change the start of `linux_positioned_iov()` (11b rewrites the `offset_high`/`flags` check). `git apply --3way` of 11b on top of this patch reports a conflict in `cpu.rs` there; the logic is compatible (11b's negative/-1 offset checks go before, the RWF_(NO)APPEND stripping stays before the `flags != 0` check). PR #128 applies cleanly on top.

> **Related work:** rvdende's fork has unmerged commits in the same area: rvdende/ginux 18b5a49f ("… pwrite on pipes and with O_APPEND", includes RWF_NOAPPEND), e360c078 ("… memfd seals and fallocate as tmpfs has them", includes KEEP_SIZE, PUNCH_HOLE|KEEP_SIZE and ftruncate error order), 12beef68 (negative pread/pwrite offsets) and 9f43c8c6 (FIFO ENXIO, among many other items). The fork's regular-file `lseek` has no SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE (only its loop block devices do, f1b02b4c). We have not compared the code line by line, and the fork is not proposed upstream. None of these commits are in `origin/main`.

A fix is offered in a PR that references this issue. Thank you for taking a look; I am happy to adjust anything.

items.title: Match Linux futex requeue, sleep and timerfd ABI details
items.body:
Fixes #103.

Several futex(2) and time syscalls diverged from Linux in ways that break common runtimes:

- futex(202) accepted only WAIT/WAKE(_BITSET). FUTEX_REQUEUE and FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE, used by musl's and older glibc's condition variables, failed with EINVAL, and so did every unknown operation. Linux do_futex() dispatches both requeue commands to futex_requeue() and rejects unknown commands, unknown operation bits and FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME outside the bitset wait with ENOSYS (kernel/futex/syscalls.c:113-118, :139-142, :161). The requeue now shares one helper with futex_requeue(456). The helper compares the source word under the futex lock (EAGAIN on mismatch, as in kernel/futex/requeue.c:478-498) and returns woken plus requeued waiters. Negative counts and a misaligned second address give EINVAL (requeue.c:400). FUTEX_WAKE_OP is still unimplemented and now reports ENOSYS.
- sys_futex() copies and validates the timeout of a timed command before futex_wait() reads the futex word (syscalls.c:192-207), so an invalid timespec is EINVAL even when the value does not match. Ginux compared the value first and returned EAGAIN.
- A timed FUTEX_WAIT with no runnable sibling returned ENOSYS. It now idles like nanosleep and reports ETIMEDOUT when the deadline passes.
- Huge but valid timespecs/timevals (tv_sec = LLONG_MAX, as used by `sleep infinity` and Rust's thread::sleep(Duration::MAX)) overflowed the nanosecond conversion and failed with EINVAL. Linux clamps them to KTIME_MAX (timespec64_to_ktime(), ktime_add_safe()). nanosleep, clock_nanosleep, both futex waits, timer_settime, setitimer and timerfd_settime now saturate.
- nanosleep/clock_nanosleep rejected an unwritable rmtp up front. Linux only writes rmtp when the sleep is interrupted and returns EFAULT then (kernel/time/hrtimer.c nanosleep_copyout()). Signal delivery to a sleeping thread now does the same instead of failing the delivery.
- clock_nanosleep accepted only REALTIME and MONOTONIC and rejected any flag bit but TIMER_ABSTIME. Linux resolves the clock first: clocks without nsleep give EOPNOTSUPP, unknown ids EINVAL (kernel/time/posix-timers.c:1387-1393), and common_nsleep() ignores other flag bits. BOOTTIME and TAI now sleep like MONOTONIC and REALTIME (as clock_gettime() maps them). MONOTONIC_RAW, the COARSE clocks, THREAD_CPUTIME and the alarm clocks give EOPNOTSUPP (the alarm clocks behave as on Linux without an RTC wakeup device). PROCESS_CPUTIME stays EINVAL (CPU-time sleeps are not implemented).
- The idle fallback of a sleep now stops once a sibling thread becomes runnable and then blocks normally. A long or infinite sleep can therefore no longer starve timed waits of other threads.
- timerfd read() required exactly 8 bytes. Linux accepts any buffer of at least 8 bytes (fs/timerfd.c:307-308).
- timerfd_settime() rejected TFD_TIMER_CANCEL_ON_SET unless the timer was absolute REALTIME, and looked up the descriptor first. Linux copies the value, checks flags and the itimerspec, then the descriptor (fs/timerfd.c:574-576, :480-486), and timerfd_setup_cancel() silently ignores CANCEL_ON_SET elsewhere.
- alarm() rounded the previous remainder up. Linux rounds to nearest and never reports a pending sub-second alarm as 0 (kernel/time/itimer.c:314-316).

The timer argument-width boot verification now also checks the setitimer saturation, CANCEL_ON_SET on a monotonic timerfd, flag checks before EBADF and a 64-byte timerfd read. Its existing alarm() expectation (2.5 s minus a little left) changes from the old round-up result 3 to Linux's 2. The linked probe (kernel/linux-probe.S) now expects ENOSYS instead of EINVAL for FUTEX_FD.

Verified with a Python/ctypes probe run on Linux 7.3 and in a python:3.13-alpine domain (before/after). All futex/time rows now match Linux except FUTEX_WAKE_OP (ENOSYS), and an interrupted sleep with a bad rmtp. The idle sleep path never delivers signals (pre-existing). nanosleep, clock_nanosleep and FUTEX_WAIT with tv_sec = LLONG_MAX now block instead of returning EINVAL. Requeue with real waiters was only checked on Linux: Python threads cannot start in that image (clone fails independently of this change). make check and tests/qemu/boot.sh (TCG) pass.

## How to verify

Branch [`fix/07-futex-requeue-sleep-timerfd`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/compare/main...meleficarumvaldis:ginux:fix/07-futex-requeue-sleep-timerfd) is based on `main` fe48e646 and applies alone.

```sh
make check
make build-verification && QEMU_ACCEL=tcg tests/qemu/boot.sh   # "Boot test passed."
```

Under KVM on AMD hosts, `tests/qemu/boot.sh` on current `main` also needs the volume-request fix ([`fix/03-withhold-first-volume-request`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/compare/main...meleficarumvaldis:ginux:fix/03-withhold-first-volume-request)); TCG does not.

Runtime behaviour, compared with Linux ([probe-07.py](https://github.com/meleficarumvaldis/ginux/blob/ginux-probes/probes/probe-07.py)):

```sh
GT_HOST=1 python3 probe-07.py > linux.out          # on Linux
/usr/local/bin/python3 probe-07.py > ginux.out    # in a python:3.13-alpine domain
diff <(grep ^GT linux.out) <(grep ^GT ginux.out)
```

Expected remaining differences and the full procedure: [VERIFY.md](https://github.com/meleficarumvaldis/ginux/blob/ginux-probes/VERIFY.md).

Thanks for taking a look. Happy to change anything that does not fit the project's direction.

items.title: Local socket queues are unbounded and uncharged: 289 MiB queued with memory-mib=8 set (36x the limit, measured)
items.body:
## Affected

c86945b1. `kernel/src/linux_socket.rs:1355-1370` (self-loopback/FIFO) and `:1409-1424` (peer path).

## Behavior

Local socket queues (unix, fast-path TCP, FIFO loopback) grow a linked list of pages with only a `checked_add` overflow guard: no byte cap, no per-domain charge; frames are `FrameOwner::KERNEL` and per the allocator the per-owner limit explicitly does not apply to the kernel owner. A writer whose peer never reads pins arbitrary physical memory.

Gate 36 (`hdae/gates-todo/36-domain-memory-accounting.md:93-98`) defines the budget as covering **private payload memory** — a socket queue is exactly that, so this is a deviation from the gate's own definition, not its documented file-cache exclusion.

## Impact (dynamically measured)

Domain configured `memory-mib=8`; fast-path pair where the accepted side floods and the connector never reads: the queue reached **289 MiB (36× the configured limit)** before the global pool was exhausted. Cross-domain amplification applies (a peer domain can grow a neighbor's queue).

## Suggested invariant

Local socket queues must be bounded and charged: count their pages against the owning domain's `memory_limit_mib` and/or enforce a byte cap per socket.

---
*Found with the [rust-in-peace](https://habr.com/ru/articles/1089374/) methodology and the [reproof](https://github.com/scadastrangelove/reproof) pipeline; verified on an isolated harness (details inline — nothing needs to be executed to evaluate). K for Kimi, G for GLM.*

items.title: Stop overlay open, rmdir and rename from destroying image files
items.body:
Fixes part of #89.

Three paths in the Linux personality silently destroyed entries of the published image (the lower layer of the runtime overlay):

- open(O_CREAT) without write access on a path that exists only in the image created an empty overlay file over it. busybox and util-linux "flock FILE" open with O_RDONLY|O_NOCTTY|O_CREAT, so "flock /etc/hostname true" emptied /etc/hostname. O_CREAT on an image directory did the same (rmdir /usr then failed with ENOTDIR).
- unlink/rmdir of an image-only path wrote a whiteout without any type or emptiness check, so "rmdir /usr/share/ca-certificates", "rmdir /usr" and "unlink /etc" succeeded and hid the whole subtree.
- rename(a, a) unlinked the target (the source itself) and then failed with EIO, deleting a. rename() also replaced directories with files and vice versa, moved directories into their own subtree, failed with ENOENT for image-only sources and left the image copy visible at the old path after moving a copied-up file.

open(O_CREAT|O_DIRECTORY) also created a regular file before failing with ENOTDIR, and O_DIRECTORY|O_TRUNC truncated a regular file before the ENOTDIR check.

Follow Linux:

- open: reject O_CREAT|O_DIRECTORY with EINVAL before any lookup (fs/open.c:1279). For an existing entry check EISDIR for O_CREAT on a directory and ENOTDIR for O_DIRECTORY on a non-directory before truncating or copying up (do_open(), fs/namei.c:4808-4822). An O_CREAT open of an existing image entry without write access opens it as is; write opens keep using the existing copy-up.
- unlink/rmdir of an image entry: apply the may_delete_dentry() type checks (fs/namei.c:3708-3713) and the simple_rmdir() emptiness check (fs/libfs.c:815) before writing the whiteout. A directory is empty only if neither the overlay nor the image has a child that is not whited out. The same merged check now also guards rmdir of an overlay directory that shadows an image directory.
- rename: same source and target is a no-op (vfs_rename(), fs/namei.c:6101); a directory moved into its own subtree is EINVAL and a target that is an ancestor of the source is ENOTEMPTY (lock_rename() traps, fs/namei.c:3894-3906); file onto directory is EISDIR, directory onto non-directory is ENOTDIR (fs/namei.c:3708-3713); a non-empty target directory is ENOTEMPTY (fs/libfs.c:882). An image-only regular file is copied up and then renamed, and the old path is whited out so the image copy does not reappear. Directories with an image layer and image symlinks return EXDEV, as overlayfs does without redirect_dir (fs/overlayfs/dir.c:1147), so mv falls back to copying.

The path-ancestry predicate lives in ginux-kernel-policy with a host unit test.

Verified with a Python/ctypes probe in a python:3.13-alpine domain (KVM) against Linux 7.3.0-rc5 on an equivalent tmpfs tree. items.title: Native scheduler counter overflow can leave a partially committed transition
items.body:
At `main` (`4c832ea6`), native scheduler transitions can mutate the selected thread/run queue and then return `RuntimeAction::Invalid` when a diagnostic `u8` counter reaches 255. The caller can retain the old trap/interrupt frame while the scheduler records a different current owner.

### Affected paths

`yield_runtime`, `preempt_runtime`, `block_runtime`, `fault_runtime`, and `exit_runtime` in [kernel/src/scheduler.rs](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/4c832ea6/kernel/src/scheduler.rs#L1762). Both the operation counter and `address_space_switches` must be checked before publishing the transition. Fault/exit also cancel blocked peers, so checking only the operation counter earlier does not make failure atomic.

### Reproduction

A host harness includes the real scheduler and `OwnedState`, with platform/domain policy stubs and serialized access to the singleton runtime. It sets the relevant counters to their boundary values, invokes each transition, and compares the run queue, selected owner, peer wait state, frame and counters before/after rejection.

On current main, 7 of 10 tests pass and 3 fail:

```
address_space_overflow_is_atomic
operation_overflow_is_atomic
peer_wakeups_are_atomic_on_both_overflows
```

This is a deterministic test of native scheduler state, not a claim that a Linux guest workload exercised these native counters.

### Expected invariant and proposed fix

A rejected transition must leave all scheduler state and the return frame unchanged. Stage the fixed-size scheduler transition, including peer cancellation, validate both counters, and publish only on success. Preserve same-address-space transitions when the switch counter is full and preserve the existing checked-overflow policy.

The proposed patch passes all 10 tests, including successful 254-to-255 boundaries, invalid contexts, failed blocks and final exit/fault. A PR with the regression harness follows.

items.title: Fix atomicity of native scheduler transitions on counter overflow
items.body:
Native `yield`, timer preemption, block, fault and exit paths can mutate scheduler state before a diagnostic counter overflow rejects the operation. Stage each transition, including blocked-peer cancellation, and publish it only after both the operation and address-space-switch counters are validated. Rejection now leaves the run queue, current owner, peer state and return frame unchanged.

Closes #82.

The existing checked-overflow policy is preserved. Same-address-space transitions still work when the switch counter is full. The staged scheduler is fixed-size and does not allocate; it adds stack-copy work that has not been benchmarked.

### Validation

- Based on current `main`, `4c832ea6`.
- `make check` passes on the Linux test host for commit `006f9b3b`.
- The new `make check-scheduler` target passes all 10 tests and is included in `make check`.
- Running the same harness against unmodified `4c832ea6` gives 7 passes and 3 failures: operation overflow, address-space-switch overflow and peer-wakeup atomicity.
- The harness includes the real scheduler and `OwnedState`; only platform/domain policy interfaces are stubbed. It is native-state evidence, not a Linux-workload overflow claim.

Full QEMU qualification is not claimed here. Earlier full-boot runs on the same rig failed both before and after the correction at Linux probe RIP 4214196 (invalid opcode after `-EINTR`), followed by a missing IOMMU marker. That separate baseline failure is not changed by this PR.

items.title: Release profile: overflow-checks not enabled (intentional?)
items.body: Question on the build profile (AI-assisted review, under my direction): [profile.release] sets panic = "abort" but has no overflow-checks key, so, unless the build passes -C overflow-checks elsewhere, release builds wrap silently on integer overflow while debug builds panic. For size/length arithmetic derived from untrusted input (e.g. archive headers), wrapping would skip the check that panics in debug. Is this intentional? If not, enabling overflow-checks = true for release, measuring the boot-time/size cost, and adding one regression test on a wrapping size computation might be worth considering. Checked at main@fbe6472e.

items.title: Offering fuzz targets for the PAX/OCI, ARP/IPv4/ICMP and volume-format parsers
items.body:
While independently reviewing ginux@82df3d71, I built libFuzzer harnesses for three untrusted-input surfaces and would like to offer them upstream:
- crates/oci tar+PAX (parse plus the traversal APIs used by published_rootfs.rs): 41.0M execs, 93.2% regions
- crates/protocol-state ARP/IPv4/ICMP: 247.1M execs, 97.5% regions
- crates/volume-format sectors: 87.8M execs, 99.4% regions
- a 15.3M-exec differential run of the PAX parser against the tar crate: all differences were fail-closed
All runs use ASan and overflow-checks, committed seeds and dictionaries; no crashes or sanitizer reports. Fuzzing only finds crashes, not logic bugs, so this is not a safety claim. The harnesses are in hafid-logic/ginux-watch (fuzz/) and consume upstream read-only at the pinned commit.
Would you prefer them under fuzz/ or tests/? A draft PR can follow if useful.

items.title: gzip ISIZE trailer sizes a ring-0 allocate+zero before validation (up to ~4 GiB per layer)
items.body:
## Summary

`install_published_layers` (kernel/src/image_store.rs:372-411) reads the expected output size from the **gzip ISIZE trailer** (u32) and performs `allocate_contiguous_extent` + `fill(0)` in ring 0 **before** decompressing; the `written == expected_length` check happens only afterwards. The store quota that would bound this is compiled out (`CACHE_QUOTA = usize::MAX`, image_store.rs:13).

## Repro (dynamic)

A 78-byte layer whose gzip trailer was patched to claim ~4 GiB:

```
ginux: OCI rootfs memory allocation failed: 4026531840 bytes
```

The kernel attempted a 3.75 GiB contiguous allocation at domain start from a 78-byte blob. Memory-safety is fine (output slice bounded, mismatch rejected) — this is purely an attacker-sized allocate+zero.

## Suggested fix

Cross-check ISIZE against the manifest-declared layer size before allocating, enforce a real cache quota, and cap per-layer output.

items.title: Bound OCI rootfs unpack allocation
items.body:
Addresses #20 without closing it.

This adds an explicit host-wide OCI rootfs unpack policy with a 512 MiB default. The install path sums gzip ISIZE values with checked arithmetic and rejects zero, overflowed, or over-limit expansion before requesting or zeroing rootfs frames. Persistent compressed-layer cache behavior is unchanged.

Verification:

- make test

Both passed locally. Please do not merge until maintainer review.

items.title: Unbounded PAX-header recursion in the OCI tar parser — kernel panic from a ~9 KB layer
items.body:
## Summary

`parse_entry` (crates/oci/src/lib.rs:712-724) recurses into the next 512-byte header for every PAX `x` entry with **no depth parameter**, and `parse_pax_overrides` accepts an empty payload. `TAR_MAX_ENTRIES` (32768) counts returned entries, not chain depth, so N chained PAX headers = N nested stack frames for 1 counted entry.

`Rootfs::parse` runs in ring 0 from `install_published_layers` (kernel/src/image_store.rs:451, and the sibling site kernel/src/published_rootfs.rs:99).

## Repro (dynamic, on a QEMU rig)

A single 9 KB gzip layer containing 4000 chained empty PAX headers + one real entry, delivered as a warm-cache image:

```
ginux: checking OCI cache docker.io/library/alpine:latest
ginux: OCI cache hit (1 layer)
GINUX_KERNEL_PANIC
```

The whole machine panics at domain start from a ~9 KB hostile layer. (Repeats a crate-level repro: the unmodified `ginux_oci::Rootfs::parse` overflows a 256 KiB stack at ~1000 headers in a release profile.)

Note the delivery vehicle: the on-volume OCI cache is integrity-only (keyless SHA-256, crates/volume-format), so a block-device writer can plant such a layer offline with zero network — worth a hardening pass of its own.

## Suggested fix

Convert the PAX-chain walk to iteration or add an explicit depth cap (e.g. 32).
